name: Contract Manufacturer

claims.claim_text: Contract manufacturing is a low-margin business. Margin can be taken at the prototype stage, but once a customer's purchasing function is involved on finished goods the price is pushed down, so the model depends on volume and utilisation rather than on markup.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not high margin, right? No one wants to give you margin
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: The attraction of contract manufacturing as a business is its cash-flow shape: a firm selling its own product must buy inventory, build an economic quantity and hold it waiting for buyers, whereas a contract shop builds nothing until an order exists and can ship before the inventory is paid for, which makes it startable without capital or a marketing operation.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't do anything until you get the order
claims.speaker: Larry Sears
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Larry Sears - Hexagram Hardware Holism

claims.claim_text: A typical assembly shop is built around two or three large accounts that make up about eighty percent of its business, with smaller work taken on top; that structure is why small jobs get fitted around the big customers' schedules.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're looking for two or three big accounts
claims.speaker: Chris Denney
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: The ideal assembly plant is laid out as a long rectangular building with receiving at one end and shipping at the other and no walls or turns in between, so that parts enter one side and finished product leaves the other.
claims.quote_verbatim: a long rectangular building
claims.speaker: Chris Denney
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: The governing question on the floor is what work can be moved off the placement machine, because anything done on the machine stops it doing its valuable work; the corollary practices are feeding and unloading automation, prepared kits and staged changeovers so the line never stops.
claims.quote_verbatim: what can I do off the machine versus what do I have to do on the machine
claims.speaker: Chris Denney
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: A board with many unique part numbers exceeds the feeder capacity of one placement machine, which is why lines run several machines in series after a single stencil print.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have a limited number of cartridges on each pick in place
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: Quoting speed is part of a manufacturer's efficiency, not separate from it: a traditional shop takes about two weeks to return a quote, while automated quoting requires a cost model built from thousands of past orders, and modelling assembly cost is much harder than modelling bare-board cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'll hear from me in two weeks
claims.speaker: Chris Denney
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: Some specialised process steps have very few dedicated providers: most assembly shops offer conformal coating in-house at small scale, but capacity and automated inspection for coating at high volume is scarce.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's not a lot of like dedicated conformal coding shops
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: In the conventional flow the customer sends files over the fence and the manufacturer checks them, sets up the placement machine and runs the job; a web-based service that makes the customer approve every part before the run inverts that responsibility.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's not how regular contract manufacturing works
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Bringing bare-board fabrication in-house is justified only to enable next-day turnkey service; going further and selling bare boards to others leads into a business with little money in it.
claims.quote_verbatim: our only goal in doing PCBs in-house is to do next-day service
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Instant online quoting from one to ten thousand units, with lead time and price returned immediately and payment by card, replaced the request-and-wait cycle for small assembly orders, initially served through a network of other people's factories.
claims.quote_verbatim: We would give you an instant quote from one to ten thousand units
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: Full-service assembly can extend past the board to buying the parts, holding inventory and drop-shipping finished units to the customer's own customers, with the whole flow driven from a web interface.
claims.quote_verbatim: buying the parts putting it together inventorying it and also drop shipping to your customers directly
claims.speaker: Stephen Craig
claims.episode_title: Mashuppery (with MEP)

claims.claim_text: The outsourcing ladder runs from buying finished assemblies from a design shop that manufactures for others, through a contract manufacturer doing varying levels of assembly and integration, to a large electronics manufacturing services firm that will also design the product.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could buy full assemblies from like, like a, from a design shop
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Inspirations and Aspirations - Recanting Rocket Rationale

claims.claim_text: An original design manufacturer is a contract manufacturer that also holds design capability in-house, offering board layout, firmware development and prototype builds, which is what distinguishes it from a pure assembly services company.
claims.quote_verbatim: ODM refers to its original design manufacturer
claims.episode_title: Standardizing Manufacturing with Pete Staples

claims.claim_text: Below about a hundred boards it is usually cheaper to assemble in-house, and above that the case for sending the work out becomes clear; at a thousand units there is no reason to be building them yourself.
claims.quote_verbatim: once you get above 100
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Photon Rich, Cash Poor

claims.claim_text: The arithmetic that settles it is time: eight hours to hand-build five boards, valued at a consultant's hourly rate, comes to roughly the price of having the same boards assembled.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is taking me at least eight hours to do five boards
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Year End, 2017

claims.claim_text: The narrow band where a personal placement machine pays for itself is around fifty boards done repeatedly; into the hundreds the work is farmed out.
claims.quote_verbatim: 50 is the pain in the ass
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Endless Y2K

claims.claim_text: For a foreign customer approaching a Chinese factory, a hundred units is the point where the factory will engage at all: they do not want the order, but they will take it on the prospect of growth.
claims.quote_verbatim: a hundred is always the number that I have in my head for like minimum order quantity
claims.speaker: Scotty Allen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scotty Allen (Strangeparts)

claims.claim_text: Below roughly a thousand units the labour content matters far less than proximity, and building domestically buys a faster design-build-test cycle, better protection of intellectual property and the ability to sit down with the shop after a short drive or domestic flight.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're building, let's say, less than 1,000 units, then potentially the labor is a lot less important
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Overseas manufacture starts to make sense at around five thousand units and above, because factories earn on volume through labour content and markup and are hard to interest below that; the offsetting advantage is a dense and diverse component supply chain concentrated in one region.
claims.quote_verbatim: the factories are a lot less interested for units under 5,000
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: The practical choice is binary: either pay more and manufacture locally, or manufacture overseas and have somebody on the ground managing it, because an unattended offshore build is the arrangement that fails.
claims.quote_verbatim: you either make the decision, pay more, get it made locally, or go to China and have somebody manage it all for you
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: A recognised trap sits between garage assembly and contract manufacture, where the volume is too large to build by hand and too small to interest a factory, and the project has not raised enough to buy its way out.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't build them in the garage anymore, but you're not really interesting for a contract manufacturer
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: That trap has a concrete shape at a few thousand units: a project at roughly twenty-five hundred pieces could not find a manufacturer willing to take the whole job, having planned around hand assembly at five hundred to a thousand.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're kind of in a no man's land with 2,500 units
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: At low volume the setup charge dominates the unit cost: twenty or thirty dollars to set a machine up, amortised across fifty boards, can exceed the selling price of a small board, which is why a company shipping many low-volume board types may assemble in-house.
claims.quote_verbatim: the setup charges alone would be more per board than what we can even sell it for
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ken Burns

claims.claim_text: A working definition of high volume in this industry is a million units shipped; below that a product is not a high-volume product regardless of how large it feels to the company making it.
claims.quote_verbatim: unless you've shipped a million of something, you're really not a high volume product
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Ghost of Keyzermas Past

claims.claim_text: Benchtop placement equipment serves the band between hand assembly and contract manufacture, covering internal prototype runs from around fifteen to a few hundred boards; once a product is stable and running, that is what contract manufacturers exist for.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's what CMS exists for
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: Designing to the set of parts a machine is already loaded with turns placement into a fast iteration loop, in the same way print orientation is designed for on a 3D printer; the constraint is tighter than a manufacturer would impose but it removes changeover entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: Can I only design boards with this set of parts?
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: The same principle applies with a subcontractor: a reasonably sized assembly house has common values already loaded, and a product can be designed around the parts sitting on the machine.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can actually design your product around the parts that they have available
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Last Minute Decisions - Obdurate Onepercenter Obstacles

claims.claim_text: Assembly houses stock common passives across the usual case sizes and will supply them from their own reels, which avoids buying a full reel for a handful of boards; the caution is that a house part may differ in temperature coefficient or power rating from the part that was specified.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got to be careful that it's not a part which you need a specific, you know, spec for
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: EE Movies, Part Rants and SPICE.

claims.claim_text: House parts also have a commercial dimension: a board built entirely from the manufacturer's own stock may earn them nothing, so specifying part numbers where the choice matters is both a technical and a relationship decision.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it's all the same resistor as the house part, you know, we may not actually make any money
claims.speaker: Chris Church
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Where the manufacturer buys the parts, the bill of materials is best exported with generic specifications rather than one manufacturer part number, with approved alternates listed in an additional column or a separate substitutes report handed over alongside it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you want the general specification rather than the specific MPN in most cases
claims.episode_title: Component Management with Jan Rychter

claims.claim_text: Larger manufacturers employ supply-chain staff whose job is continuity: making sure jelly-bean parts have several qualified alternates specified in the design, and flagging single-sourced components early, because a manufacturer may need to build a line or open a factory to meet a demand ramp and that cannot be started late.
claims.quote_verbatim: so that you have supply chain continuity
claims.speaker: Jeff Kaiser
claims.episode_title: Merry Keyzermas!

claims.claim_text: When a component becomes unobtainable during a build, the design house may buy the scarce parts itself and supply them free of charge to the manufacturer so the run can continue, and has to explain to the client that a finished, paid-for design can still be unmanufacturable.
claims.quote_verbatim: We can't get these Hiroshi connectors
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: Contract manufacturers now absorb a large part of design finishing: a half-built product can be handed over and the manufacturer will complete the design-for-manufacture work and the enclosure.
claims.quote_verbatim: A lot of CMs you can give half-baked products to
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: Those manufacturers rarely do that work themselves: their speciality is the assembly line, so board layout and enclosure design are farmed out to independent designers, which is where a substantial share of contract layout work originates.
claims.quote_verbatim: their speciality is the manufacturing side of things
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: Consultants also pick up work through manufacturers directly, because a manufacturer's clients hit obsolete parts and board problems and need someone to fix them; distributor field engineers are a second referral channel.
claims.quote_verbatim: contract manufacturers. I've gotten work through them
claims.speaker: Eric Thompson
claims.episode_title: Electronics Consultant Impedance Matching

claims.claim_text: The risk in handing everything to a turnkey supplier appears at the exit: a manufacturer that did all the design work may refuse to release the data needed to move production elsewhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: when they try to get the info back out of them so they can take it somewhere else, no, sir
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: Asking a supplier in advance for the full set of process limits does not produce them; the only reliable way to learn what a process can actually do, as opposed to its stated safe limits, is to build the thing.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only way to really get the answer is to actually build it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: A manufacturer that quietly works around a design problem at prototype quantities, for instance by hand-soldering a part that the machine cannot place, leaves the fault to surface at volume when the same shop declines the order; feedback about what will not scale is what separates a good manufacturer from a poor one.
claims.quote_verbatim: they sort of like hand soldered that part
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: Design-for-manufacture review by the assembler catches problems before the first build, such as vias inside a fine-pitch package, and that feedback is a service customers routinely forget they are entitled to.
claims.quote_verbatim: in your QFN you have these, you know, like buried vias or whatever
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: That review also catches elementary errors, such as a footprint whose name says one case size while the parts ordered against it are another.
claims.quote_verbatim: parts that have 0805 in the name do not fit on top of 0402
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Garbage Ninjas

claims.claim_text: The handoff has to be complete and confident, because changes after it are where the manufacturer earns margin; the informal loop of walking onto the floor to clarify a detail with a manufacturing engineer does not exist once production is external.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's how they're making their margins is like, oh, well you need that changed
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Inspirations and Aspirations - Recanting Rocket Rationale

claims.claim_text: Revision identifiers become load-bearing once an outside party is building: a designation has to be unique and specific enough to serve as an address that both sides can point at, which informal descriptions of a revision and its firmware do not provide.
claims.quote_verbatim: having like something where it's an actual unique identifier
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Ludicrously High Frequency Interference

claims.claim_text: Manufacturers act on revision changes through the part numbering, routing the change to the responsible team, updating the placement job and adjusting test coverage accordingly.
claims.quote_verbatim: the contract manufacturer will take that information and they'll see the rev change
claims.episode_title: Product Lifecycle Management with Michael Corr

claims.claim_text: Arranging a contract build has its own lead time of five to ten days before anything is made, which is why a schedule measured in days forces an in-house build regardless of cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: it takes five or 10 days just to arrange that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: A very small paid run, even four assembled boards with the manufacturer sourcing all the parts, works as a rehearsal: it exercises the handoff and returns the same kind of feedback a higher-volume manufacturer would give, for a cost of around twelve hundred dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've decided to actually get a contract manufacturer to assemble four for us
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ludicrously High Frequency Interference

claims.claim_text: A pilot order of a few dozen units before committing to volume is the standard way to test both the product and the supplier.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's why I'm ordering 50 up front right now
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Secret Squirrel

claims.claim_text: Pilot quantity is usually set by cash rather than by demand: one funded project's largest pilot was five hundred pieces sold at cost, with quotes gathered across volumes to model what gross margin would become at scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: the biggest pilot run we did using phase one money, um, was 500 pieces
claims.speaker: Zach Fredin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Fredin

claims.claim_text: Those models are fragile to supply-side events: a vendor acquisition doubled the price of one project's processor and raised its bill of materials by ten percent.
claims.quote_verbatim: the cost of my processor doubled and that increased my bomb cost by 10%
claims.speaker: Zach Fredin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Fredin

claims.claim_text: Referral is the practical way to find a manufacturer, because it borrows someone else's filtering; a supplier that performs is then kept across projects rather than re-tendered.
claims.quote_verbatim: referrals are the right way to go
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: Bidding a job to several shops and letting one win repeatedly produces a partner rather than a vendor: the relationship reaches the point where odd requests, including builds the customer had intended to do themselves, are simply absorbed.
claims.quote_verbatim: I bid out to a few different places usually
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dave Young

claims.claim_text: Time should not be spent persuading a manufacturer to take work it does not want; a shop that says it will not talk until the customer is spending a million dollars a year is doing both parties a favour by saying so.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't waste time trying to convince the contract manufacturer to do something they don't want to do
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dave Young

claims.claim_text: Stating the volume trajectory honestly at the outset, as ten boards now with the hope of hundreds and then thousands, makes suppliers self-select quickly instead of discovering the mismatch later.
claims.quote_verbatim: I know that I'm going to buy 10 boards from you
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dave Young

claims.claim_text: Matching the manufacturer's size to the job matters more than finding the best one: very small subcontractors disappear when they lose a single customer, large ones will not take small jobs, and a small customer cannot buy priority by offering to pay double because the interruption is not worth the shop's while.
claims.quote_verbatim: the really small ones generally just disappear
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Harrison - X-ray Examining Xenogogue

claims.claim_text: Sending a small company to a tier-one manufacturer because a large brand uses it is a bad decision, and it is the kind of advice that circulates from people who have not run the process themselves.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's a very bad decision for a small company to use a large, you know, tier one CM
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: Manufacturing houses differ in what they are actually good at, and that specialisation is not visible from outside, which is the main difficulty for a first-time customer trying to choose one.
claims.quote_verbatim: Different manufacturing houses have different capabilities
claims.speaker: Alvaro And Jen From The Ure
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Some smaller houses invest engineering time in promising startups without charge for a set number of iterations, treating it as a bet that the customer will become a volume account.
claims.quote_verbatim: They will work on your project for X number of iterations
claims.speaker: Alvaro And Jen From The Ure
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Assembly capability clusters geographically around a large former employer, so a region that once hosted a major manufacturer still supports several independent board shops within a short drive.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have a behemoth former company nearby that usually helps to sprout up a lot of like supporting companies
claims.speaker: Jared Wolff
claims.episode_title: Cellular IoT with Jared Wolff

claims.claim_text: Domestic assembly splits between quality-certified shops built around ISO and aerospace standards and small scrappy shops with a maker mindset; a shop in the second group has to decide whether it wants to compete for pennies, knowing that volume work tends to move offshore regardless.
claims.quote_verbatim: once the volumes get up, it's just going to go overseas anyway
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ken Burns

claims.claim_text: Local capacity can be substantial without being enormous: two assemblers in one region were enough to build up to two hundred thousand units a year, sufficient to carry three product lines before expansion was needed.
claims.quote_verbatim: we can manufacture up to 200,000 units per year
claims.speaker: Christina Cyr
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Christina Cyr

claims.claim_text: Miniaturisation left domestic capability behind in some regions: houses that once built large consumer electronics can still handle small volumes but not extreme ones, which is what pushes work to a nearby lower-cost country or overseas.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can handle small volumes out here. They can't handle extraordinarily large volumes
claims.speaker: Alvaro And Jen From The Ure
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: For a first batch it is almost always better to build somewhere the team can walk down the street and look at it, because the first batch of a new product is where the problems are.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's almost always better to, you know, do it somewhere where you can just walk down the street and see it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Josh Lifton

claims.claim_text: Being physically at the factory is what closes the loop: customers who fly over achieve a great deal in a week and then stall the moment they leave, so momentum depends on either continuous presence or a knowledgeable representative on the ground.
claims.quote_verbatim: just being a physical presence right at the factory
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: The designer's presence carries authority that a representative's does not: with the person who can approve a change standing on the line, decisions that would take days or weeks happen in an afternoon, and factories unused to dealing with the designer respond with a high level of support.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can have things that happen in an afternoon that normally would have taken days or even weeks
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Merry Keyzermas!

claims.claim_text: Factory visits matter most when nothing is going wrong: a smoothly running programme invites complacency, and the things to verify in person are that the line has not been moved somewhere worse and that the account still has priority.
claims.quote_verbatim: You want to make sure that your line hasn't been like relocated to the basement
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Ghost of Keyzermas Past

claims.claim_text: The assumption that a factory will fix an unfinished design is the recurring failure of first-time hardware companies: factories employ engineers, but there is no reason to expect them to be better than the customer's own, and trusting an unknown party to redesign a board is a risk taken blind.
claims.quote_verbatim: China will fix it, and it will magically become a product
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe Grand - Pancyclopaedic Prototyping Polymath

claims.claim_text: An unsupervised factory may substitute components it has a supply relationship for, or buy through a broker carrying counterfeit or poor-quality parts; the resulting failures appear months later at volume, when tracing the cause backwards through a thousand fielded units is close to impossible.
claims.quote_verbatim: a factory might swap in different capacitors because they have a relationship with the company
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe Grand - Pancyclopaedic Prototyping Polymath

claims.claim_text: Recovering money from a manufacturer for its own error is close to impossible; the realistic best outcome is that they agree to fix it in their own time, which costs the customer a week or two of schedule.
claims.quote_verbatim: trying to extract money back out of them is next to impossible
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Motors And Upgrading Sinclairs - Adapting Apraxiated Automobiles

claims.claim_text: The relationship runs both ways and can be ended by the supplier, whether because the account is too small to be worth keeping or because of friction with particular people at the customer.
claims.quote_verbatim: The contract manufacturer has told us to piss off
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Google Glass & Adafruit - Obtaining Ostentatious Oculiforms

claims.claim_text: The worst event on a contract line is the line going down, because every idle day costs money and earns none for either party; a stoppage can justify flying an engineer in from wherever they are, and one took four days on site to clear.
claims.quote_verbatim: the worst thing that can happen when you're running a manufacturing line with a contract manufacturer is the line going down
claims.speaker: Nash Reilly
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Nash Reilly

claims.claim_text: Sustaining engineering is the function that owns fielded product: tracking return trends, finding root cause, designing the failure mode out, and keeping the supply chain stable as volumes and vendor relationships change.
claims.quote_verbatim: sustaining engineering is like when you have a field return issue
claims.speaker: Nash Reilly
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Nash Reilly

claims.claim_text: Placing acceptance testing at the manufacturer keeps failing boards inside the factory, which gives the manufacturer its own reason to fix the process because it wants high yield; yield has to be monitored, and failures escaping to the customer mean a test is missing.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you can make all the boards that's not working getting stuck at the cm they will take care of their process because they want high yield
claims.speaker: Fredrik Kensander
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: A security step delegated to the manufacturer as a final production action can silently not happen: a shipped consumer device was found with its debug interface unlocked because locking it had been pushed to the contract manufacturer.
claims.quote_verbatim: that was pushed to our contract manufacturer
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Shouting at chips with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: A field failure traced through several layers of subcontracting showed how remote assembly compounds small differences: the cable assembly was subcontracted, the connector housings used were not the specified Molex parts, their weaker keying let assembly workers mate the connector reversed, and one reversed orientation killed the first LED driver in the chain. A protection resistor would have prevented it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the connector housings they used, which weren't Molex, were much easier to plug into the connector the wrong way around
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: 3 Cent Micros And 1000s of LEDs

claims.claim_text: Ordering a custom part from a factory for decades without ever holding the design data means having no design control: when the individual who arranged the original order leaves, the customer cannot reproduce a part it has shipped in every product.
claims.quote_verbatim: They never had design control
claims.speaker: David Ray
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: Large manufacturers employ engineers whose entire career is finding out why components do not solder correctly; a small company scaling up has none of that, and a defect appearing on a few percent of tens of thousands of boards consumes the company in rework rather than production.
claims.quote_verbatim: why components don't solder correctly
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Ardui...no Dave This Week?

claims.claim_text: Blaming a vanished contract manufacturer is a common account of a failed crowdfunded hardware project, and the underlying error is treating funding as the end of the work rather than the start of a process that has to be supervised.
claims.quote_verbatim: we gave all your money to the contract manufacturer and they just disappeared
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, IndieGoGo & Ignite - Jasperated Jimswinger Jobbery

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunded hardware projects attract unsolicited offers from overseas firms proposing to handle everything for around a tenth of the money raised, and full-service arrangements of that kind are quoted at ten to fifteen percent.
claims.quote_verbatim: we'll give us 10% of your Kickstarter money
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Milling About

claims.claim_text: Design work moving to external manufacturers costs younger engineers the experience of seeing production, which was previously how they learned why a board behaves the way it does.
claims.quote_verbatim: you kind of lose a lot of that as well for younger engineers
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Taylor - Multi-talented Meter Maker

claims.claim_text: Small process improvements come from proximity: an engineer next to the line notices that moving a resistor would ease assembly or stop a capacitor cracking, and an external manufacturer has no comparable incentive to feed that back.
claims.quote_verbatim: a CM just wouldn't be as invested in that kind of thing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dave Young

claims.claim_text: Engineers and product companies outsource earlier than they should: there is a range of volume a team could build itself that improves both its ability to ship and its understanding of its own product, and moving to a second manufacturer too quickly ended one working relationship.
claims.quote_verbatim: engineers and product companies jump to outsourcing stuff way too early
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Spencer Wright

claims.claim_text: Keeping assembly in-house buys just-in-time building: instead of ordering five hundred or a thousand boards that sit as inventory for months, production can run a couple of days ahead of orders with parts bought against demand under a bonded inventory arrangement.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could just be basically building to order
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Choosing placement equipment badly is a due-diligence failure with a known remedy: open channels with several vendors at once, have the actual board built on the actual machine before buying, and prefer machines that manufacturers run in daily production.
claims.quote_verbatim: select a machine that actual CEMs use every day in production
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: A machine that can place a small part but does so slowly still costs throughput, adding a large fraction to the time per board purely for placement precision, which is a cost that is easy to miss when comparing specifications.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to take, you know, 80% more time per board to do it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Choosing the smallest possible parts to make a product compact narrows the field of manufacturers that can build it, which is a cost of miniaturisation that is not obvious at design time.
claims.quote_verbatim: that rules out many contract manufacturers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Cheap placement machines built on stepper motors instead of closed-loop encoders cannot hold placement accuracy; accuracy is what costs money in this equipment, and the decision includes the hassle of learning and maintaining the machine rather than only its purchase price.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're trying to use stepper motors to do things that you really need a closed loop system for
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Hirschman of PCB:NG

claims.claim_text: Because boards are never perfectly flat or square, a placement machine needs a vision system: a few thousandths of an inch of misalignment decides whether a passive lands on its pad or tombstones.
claims.quote_verbatim: You have to have a vision system
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: Placement lines carry ongoing costs beyond the machine: floor space, noise, and hours spent programming; one owner sold an entire line and moved the work to contract manufacturers on that basis.
claims.quote_verbatim: One of my friends just recently sold an entire pick and place line because it takes up way too much room
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: It's a Keyzermas Miracle!

claims.claim_text: Working through a subcontractor imposes a documentation burden that in-house assembly avoids, which is itself a reason short-run shops keep placement in-house.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got so much documentation to do
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: Meracious Mike Manuduction

claims.claim_text: Enclosure machining is best bought from the manufacturer that assembles the product, because routing cases through a third party adds receiving and shipping steps and its own minimum volumes, and a design change then strands the punched stock.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you get a third party to do it, then you've got handling issues
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Gouging Green Gardyloo

claims.claim_text: Designing for volume is largely a negotiation about what to give up: which compromises on shape, form and function are acceptable in order to be manufacturable, settled before samples are requested from bidding factories.
claims.quote_verbatim: what compromises are we willing to make on the shape and form and functionality of this product to be able to manufacture it
claims.speaker: Simone Giertz
claims.episode_title: Product Design with Simone Giertz

claims.claim_text: Production ramps in stages: the first builds are run by the design engineers alongside the manufacturer, more staff are trained as volume grows so the designers are not permanently on site, and once units are in the field the difficult failures route back to the design team.
claims.quote_verbatim: the first builds is going to be the design engineers for the CM
claims.speaker: Alvaro Prieto
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Manufacturers relocate operations between countries to protect their own margins, which makes a customer's production location a moving target rather than a settled decision.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're going to go and try and find the best deal because they have to make their margins
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Vertically Integrated Design Engineering

claims.claim_text: A manufacturer without its own factory can be forced into owning one: partners could not deliver the required quality at modest and bursty volumes, and a customer needing a hundred thousand units before Christmas and nothing for nine months afterwards is a lot of disruption for little payoff to a factory. Getting into manufacturing is easy and getting out of it is what is hard.
claims.quote_verbatim: Getting into manufacturing is actually not so difficult. Getting out of it is what's difficult
claims.episode_title: Standardizing Manufacturing with Pete Staples

claims.claim_text: Co-investing with a manufacturer to build its capability let a small company buy at a cost curve normally reserved for very high volumes, and gave it predictable build-to-build costs it could plan hiring and new designs around.
claims.quote_verbatim: we co-invested with them to help grow the capability
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: Handing the complete build, including part purchasing, to the manufacturer is a continuity measure: production and customer supply continue if the founder is unavailable, and lot sizes as small as ten finished units can be run that way.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm fully turning everything over to my manufacturer
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Parts going missing inside a factory is a tracking problem rather than a loss problem, and it is solved by extending the customer's own inventory system to follow components through the manufacturer's process.
claims.quote_verbatim: I actually have worked with my contract manufacturer to track parts through the factory
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: AI Tooling with Matt Liberty and Luke Beno

claims.claim_text: Very small overseas runs can be cheaper than local ones because of the non-recurring engineering charge rather than the unit price, with one supplier quoting about a hundred dollars for setup on runs of five or ten units.
claims.quote_verbatim: China's NRE fee was like $100 or something
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin O'Flynn - Aspirated Adamantine Attacks

claims.claim_text: Automation has narrowed the cost gap for mid-volume assembly, to the point that two good local manufacturers can cover runs in the thousands without the advantage of offshore labour applying.
claims.quote_verbatim: the cost advantage of going to China is sort of going away
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Bare-board suppliers in some markets bundle free common components and assembly with an order for boards, provided the design uses generic parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: they will give you free connectors, free resistors
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: What's In A Name?

claims.claim_text: Kits are hard to justify as a product where local contract assembly is cheap: the assembled board carries a working guarantee the kit cannot, and short-form kits with the surface-mount work already done are the surviving middle ground.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's so cheap to get it locally contract manufactured
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A 2013 Recap - Year-end Yarn Yakking

claims.claim_text: A very simple board, on the order of five parts and all through-hole, is one of the few cases where contract assembly is not worth arranging.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it's a board with five parts or something
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A 2013 Recap - Year-end Yarn Yakking

claims.claim_text: Retailers of third-party designs work either by having the designer manufacture and sell through them, or by manufacturing the design in-house under a royalty to the designer.
claims.quote_verbatim: we will take their design with their, you know, blessing, of course, uh, manufacture it in house and then give them a royalty on it
claims.speaker: Chris Taylor
claims.episode_title: An Interview with the SparkFun Team - Efficacious Engineering Ensemble

claims.claim_text: Fine-pitch BGA packages are a manufacturability constraint that narrows supplier choice: the qualifying question for a manufacturer becomes whether it can place that part reliably on every board.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've found a good, uh, CM who knows how to, you know, put this down reliably
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein
